The experimental protocol was approved by the Emory University Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided written informed consent.

These procedures were part of a larger project in which participants completed two sessions that differed in medication state ("OFF" and "ON" their typical dopaminergic medications), separated by approximately one week, with session order counterbalanced across participants; data from the ONmedication sessions will be reported separately.

Participants were categorized as FoG+ (n = 13) if FoG was documented in their clinical record or self-reported on the NFOG-Q (total score > 0); all other participants with PD were classified as FoG-(n = 16).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Freezing of gait (FoG) is among the most disabling symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) and is associated with balance impairment and increased falls risk, yet remains challenging to understand due to its episodic and context-dependent nature.

Altered supplementary motor area (SMA) function at rest and before self-initiated movements has been implicated in FoG; however, whether this extends to functionally relevant balance behavior is unknown.
A loss of balance in response to support surface translations during standing elicits a perturbation-evoked N1 potential, an error assessment signal linked to SMA activity.
We therefore predicted that people with FoG would have smaller and later N1 responses than people with PD without FoG and older adults.

We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) during backward support-surface translations in 29 people with PD (71 ± 7 years), including 13 people with a history of FoG (FoG+) and 16 people without FoG (FoG-), and 26 older adults (OA; 67 ± 6 years).
N1 amplitude and latency were quantified at a central midline electrode and defined as the largest negative peak 100-300 ms post-perturbation.
N1 responses were similar between OA and FoG-(∆ = 4.0 µV and 2.8 ms, respectively).
In contrast, FoG+ had smaller N1 amplitudes than FoG-(∆ = 18.1 µV, p = 0.001) and OA (∆ = 14.1 µV, p = 0.003), and both differences persisted after adjusting for age.

FoG+ also had later N1 latencies than OA (∆ = 26.5 ms, p = 0.029), with a similar but non-significant difference versus FoG-(∆ = 23.6 ms, p = 0.091); after adjusting for age, these latency differences were not retained.
These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked cortical activity is altered in FoG, potentially reflecting altered SMA function, and may provide a functionally relevant marker of FoG susceptibility.

Freezing of gait (FoG) is one of the most disabling features of Parkinson's disease (PD) and is associated with increased fall risk (Okuma et al., 2018; Perez-Lloret et al., 2014), yet how neural processes for mobility differ in individuals with and without FoG remains poorly understood.

text.text: Although FoG manifests episodically, susceptibility to freezing may also reflect differences in neural processes that are evident even outside overt freezing episodes.

For instance, even outside of freezing episodes, individuals with FoG exhibit poorer gait (Barbe et al., 2014; Glover et al., 2020), balance (Bekkers et al., 2017), and cognitive function (Monaghan et al., 2023) than those without a history of freezing, although the extent of these impairments varies across individuals.

text.text: Identifying objective physiological markers of FoG susceptibility could improve our mechanistic understanding and inform the development of targeted assessments and interventions.

Dysfunction across widespread cortical and subcortical networks has been implicated in FoG, with many studies implicating the supplementary motor area (SMA) as an important node within these networks.

The SMA is extensively connected with cortical and subcortical regions and contributes to internally generated movement, motor preparation, task switching, response inhibition, and balance control (de Lima-Pardini et al., 2020; Jacobs et al., 2009; Nachev et al., 2008; Rahimpour et al., 2022).

Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has enabled measurement of cortical activity during actual locomotion, revealing altered recruitment of SMA and other frontal motor regions during FoG-provoking tasks such as turning and doorway passage, even in the absence of overt freezing episodes (Cockx et al., 2024).

text.text: If FoG reflects a reduced capacity of SMA-implicated networks to process and respond to such changes, then people with FoG may exhibit altered perturbationevoked cortical responses during balance control.
Here, we measured perturbation-evoked N1 responses using EEG during standing support-surface translations in people with PD with FoG (FoG+), people with PD without FoG (FoG-), and older adults.

We predicted that FoG+ would have smaller N1 amplitudes than FoG-and older adults, reflecting reduced SMA engagement, and later N1 latencies, consistent with delayed N1 responses in populations with impaired balance (Duckrow, 1999; Palmer et al., 2025).

text.text: Participants underwent a series of standing balance perturbations while EEG was continuously recorded (Section 2.6).
Participants stood barefoot with their feet approximately hip-width apart and wore an overhead safety harness.
Before testing, participants completed a familiarization block of backward perturbations to ensure that they could recover balance without taking a step.
Participants then underwent approximately 45 pairs of backward support-surface translation perturbations (7.5 cm, 15 cm/s, 0.01 m/s 2 ) with their eyes closed.
After each pair, participants verbally reported whether the second perturbation was in the same or a different direction from the first.
In each pair, the first perturbation was directed directly backward and occurred at an unpredictable time.
The second perturbation occurred 4 s later and was directed posterolateral to the left or right.
Following the participant's response, the platform returned to its initial position without lateral displacement to avoid providing additional directional information.
Intertrial intervals ranged from approximately 10 to 60 s.
Seated rest breaks were taken every 15 trials or sooner if requested.

Here, we observed differences in perturbation-evoked cortical activity between people with PD with and without FoG during a functionally relevant balance task.

Although the reactive balance task did not elicit overt freezing episodes, people with FoG demonstrated smaller N1 amplitudes and tended to have later N1 latencies than both people without FoG and older adults, with amplitude differences persisting after adjusting for age.

In contrast, people with PD without FoG showed N1 responses similar to older adults, suggesting that altered cortical activity in PD may be more closely associated with FoG status than with PD diagnosis alone, and highlight the value of considering FoG status when examining cortical activity in PD.

Importantly, these differences were evident even in the absence of a freezing episode, suggesting that perturbation-evoked cortical activity may capture neurophysiological differences associated with susceptibility to FoG.
FoG-related alterations in cortical activity may extend beyond voluntary movement to processes involved in responding to unexpected balance disturbances.

Reduced cortical potentials associated with motor preparation have been observed in people with FoG compared to older adults during voluntary lower-limb movement and gait initiation (Karimi et al., 2021; Marquez et al., 2023).

Our findings extend prior work by identifying smaller N1 responses following unexpected balance disturbances in people with FoG, which may reflect altered cortical processes involved in rapidly evaluating and responding to unexpected balance disturbances.

Consistent with this interpretation, both perturbationevoked N1 responses and midfrontal theta activity (3-7 Hz), a marker of action monitoring (Luu et al., 2000), increase following a loss of balance, scaling with both the magnitude of the perturbation and need for corrective motor responses (Solis-Escalante et al., 2021).

text.text: Together with smaller perturbation-evoked N1 potentials observed here, these findings suggest that people with FoG may have altered cortical processes associated with action monitoring that limits the ability to evaluate and response to balance perturbations.
Our findings support the hypothesis that FoG is associated with altered SMA and broader motornetwork function, even without overt freezing episodes.
In neurotypical adults, source localization analyses indicate that the perturbation-evoked balance N1 is dominated by a central midline cortical source encompassing the SMA (Protzak et al., 2026).

text.text: Although source localization is beyond the scope of the present study, our findings of altered perturbation-evoked cortical activity in people with freezing are consistent with neuroimaging evidence implicating altered SMA activity and connectivity in FoG.

Altered connectivity between the SMA and cortical and subcortical locomotor regions further suggests that FoG reflects dysfunction of a distributed motor network rather than the SMA in isolation (Bardakan et al., 2022; Fling et al., 2014; Song et al., 2021).

text.text: One potentially relevant circuit is the hyperdirect pathway, through which the SMA and other frontal regions project directly to the subthalamic nucleus (STN) to rapidly modify or suppress motor output (Nambu et al., 2002).

text.text: Altered cortical-STN signaling and recruitment of stopping-related circuitry have been implicated in FoG, particularly during challenging gait conditions such as turning and doorway passage (Cockx et al., 2024; Gilat et al., 2015; Matar et al., 2019).

text.text: Thus, smaller N1 responses in FoG+ may reflect broader SMA-centered network dysfunction rather than isolated SMA dysfunction.
Future studies combining EEG source localization with measures of cortical-subcortical connectivity could clarify the neural circuits underlying these altered responses.
Later perturbation-evoked N1 latencies may reflect slower cortical processing of balance-related information.

This interpretation is consistent with the broader ERP literature, in which longer component latencies have been associated with slower stimulus evaluation and information processing (Pinal et al., 2015a; Terrasa et al., 2018), whereas ERP amplitude can reflect the magnitude of neural resource allocation or engagement during stimulus processing (Pinal et al., 2015b; Sachs et al., 2004).

text.text: However, the latency differences observed here should be interpreted cautiously.
Although N1 latency was later in FoG+ than in older adults, the difference between FoG+ and FoG-did not reach statistical significance.
Moreover, group differences in N1 latency were attenuated after adjusting for age, which was itself a significant predictor of latency, and the FoG+ group was older than OA.
Thus, later N1 responses may reflect age-related slowing of cortical processing rather than a FoG-specific alteration.

Interpretation of N1 latency is further complicated because many individuals in the FoG+ group had atypical perturbation-evoked morphologies, with multiple small deflections often present within the N1 time window (100-300 ms post-perturbation) rather than a single well-defined peak.
Thus, it is unclear whether latency estimates in FoG+ reflect true differences in response timing or are influenced by differences in overall waveform morphology.
Because people with FoG also demonstrated poorer balance, the smaller N1 responses observed in this group could reflect greater overall impairment rather than FoG status specifically.
However, FoG+ and FoG-had similar disease duration, motor symptom severity, global cognition, and set-shifting.
Prior work has associated N1 amplitude with individual differences in cognitive set-shifting and balance-related function in older adults (Payne et al., 2022).

text.text: However, N1 amplitude was not associated with balance or set-shifting function within either PD group in the present study.

One possible explanation is that the same perturbation magnitude represented different levels of balance challenge across individuals, which can influence cortical responses to perturbations (Kerr et al., 2026; Payne and Ting, 2020).

text.text: Alternatively, N1 amplitude may capture only one of several neural processes contributing to individual differences in clinical function.
In contrast to the lack of association with clinical balance function, larger N1 amplitudes were associated with greater perceived balance confidence on the ABC Scale in people with FoG.
This direction is opposite to that reported in neurotypical older adults, in whom larger N1 amplitudes were associated with lower balance confidence (Payne et al., 2022).

text.text: This distinction may be clinically relevant because discordance between perceived and objective balance ability has been independently associated with fall history in people with PD, suggesting that perceived balance provides information not fully captured by performance-based measures (Longhurst et al., 2025a (Longhurst et al., , 2025b)).

text.text: These findings suggest that the relationships between brain activity and clinical characteristics may differ by FoG status; however, given the small sample and exploratory nature of this analysis, these findings should be replicated before drawing mechanistic conclusions.
Despite group-level differences in N1 amplitude, individual variability suggests that perturbation-evoked cortical activity does not map simply onto binary FoG status.
This variability is consistent with the clinical and pathophysiological heterogeneity of FoG and the episodic nature of its presentation.

In this study, one individual in the FoG-group had an N1 amplitude more than 1.5 SD below the FoG-mean, within the range observed in FoG+, whereas one FoG+ participant had an N1 amplitude nearly 3 SD above the FoG+ mean, exceeding the FoG-mean.

This variability may reflect heterogeneity in freezing phenotype (e.g., levodoparesponsive versus levodopa-unresponsive FoG), the presence or absence of postural instability, cognitive status, or diagnostic classification (Bekkers et al., 2017; McKay et al., 2019; Nonnekes et al., 2015).

text.text: Larger and more diverse cohorts will be needed to determine whether perturbation-evoked cortical responses can distinguish established FoG from prodromal vulnerability to freezing, or whether they are better conceptualized as markers of a broader balance-cognitive phenotype associated with freezing risk.

Taken together, perturbation-evoked cortical activity may provide a sensitive and functionally relevant neurophysiological signal for identifying freezing-related balance dysfunction and warrants further study in larger cohorts.

Given the N1 is elicited during a functionally relevant balance task that engages cognitive, affective, and sensorimotor processes, it may be capable of capturing distinct mechanisms recruited during freezing in real-world settings compared to stationary laboratory paradigms.

This capability is particularly relevant given that freezing categorization varies with the measure used (Duysens and Smits-Engelsman, 2026), and subjective self-reports do not always align with episodes observed in the laboratory or clinic due to the transient and context-dependent nature of freezing (Gilat et al., 2026).
